name: Field
label: Design & Development
summary: A token pipeline that turns Figma variables into production CSS without a handoff gap.
problem: Product teams were shipping three slightly different greys, two radii, and a documentation site nobody trusted.
approach: I mapped tokens to a typed source of truth, rebuilt the component set as code-first primitives, and documented usage as working examples.
outcome: One system across web and native. Designers edit variables; engineers consume the same names.

name: Signal
label: Interaction & Development
summary: An observability console that makes incident response feel like reading, not decoding.
problem: On-call engineers were switching between four dashboards to answer one question: what broke, and for whom.
approach: I designed a single timeline with density controls, then implemented the layout so charts, logs, and traces share one scroll context.
outcome: Mean time to first useful signal dropped. The UI is quiet until something actually matters.

name: North
label: Design & Development
summary: Wayfinding for a city transit network — maps you can hold, not just look at.
problem: The existing app treated stations as pins. People needed sequences, transfers, and time, not geography.
approach: I rebuilt the core loop around trips, not maps. The map became a supporting layer; the itinerary became the product.
outcome: A prototype that operations and design could both use in workshops. Shipped as the new trip model.

name: Ledger
label: Design & Development
summary: A treasury workspace for operators who live in numbers and cannot afford decoration.
problem: Finance tools either looked like spreadsheets from 2009 or like consumer banking with the data hidden.
approach: Dense, tabular, but with typographic hierarchy and reversible actions. I designed and built the first production screens.
outcome: Operators keep the density. New hires understand the page without a walkthrough.

name: Draft
label: Design & Development
summary: A spec tool where comments attach to the actual UI, not a screenshot in a thread.
problem: Feedback lived in Figma, Slack, and tickets. Engineering never knew which version was current.
approach: I prototyped annotated live views: the component is the document. Comments, states, and acceptance criteria sit on the same surface.
outcome: A working prototype used internally to replace status meetings with a single source of review.
